plan.topic: Strength training while taking tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound): how much of the weight lost is lean mass, why muscle matters for metabolic health and function, and a guideline-based plan to start
plan.angle: Evergreen 'where to start' deep-dive. Hook: muscle preservation is in the news (UNC Health '5 habits on a GLP-1', Oct 15). Body: (1) what lean mass vs fat mass means and how a DXA scan measures it, noting that lean mass isn't pure muscle; (2) SURMOUNT-1 DXA substudy: about three-quarters of the weight lost was fat mass, in adults with obesity, or overweight with a weight-related condition, without diabetes. Give per-arm figures and the timeframe from the paper; (3) why some lean-mass loss happens with any weight loss, including diet-only and bariatric comparisons from the literature, labelled as separate studies; (4) what the guidelines recommend: muscle-strengthening activity at least 2 days a week (WHO / US Physical Activity Guidelines), starting gently, a beginner progression using bodyweight, bands and machines; (5) protein at each meal from a variety of foods, per the 2025 joint nutrition advisory, unless your clinician has told you to limit protein (e.g. kidney disease); (6) training around common GI side effects: eat slowly, fluids unless you've been told to limit fluids; (7) questions for your prescriber, a dietitian or a physical therapist. Habits are 'recommended', never 'proven on tirzepatide'. No dosing. Close with the full prescriber line.

package.description:
Quick answer: In SURMOUNT-1's DXA scans (adults with obesity, or overweight with a weight-related condition, without diabetes), about 1/4 of weight lost on tirzepatide was lean mass, which isn't only muscle.
WHO and US guidelines recommend strength training on 2+ days a week for adults in general (start gently); it hasn't been proven to protect muscle on tirzepatide specifically.
Common side effects are digestive (e.g. nausea, diarrhea, constipation). Kidney disease? Check before adding protein.

This content is for educational purposes only and is not medical advice. Don't stop or change your current medicines on your own. Tirzepatide is a prescription medicine — talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

Sources:
1. Jastreboff AM et al. Tirzepatide Once Weekly for the Treatment of Obesity (SURMOUNT-1). NEJM, 2022. https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2206038
2. WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour. WHO, 2020. https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789240015128
3. Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition. HHS, 2018. https://odphp.health.gov/sites/default/files/2019-09/Physical_Activity_Guidelines_2nd_edition.pdf
4. Mozaffarian D et al. Nutritional priorities to support GLP-1 therapy for obesity: a joint Advisory. AJCN, 2025. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajcnut.2025.04.023

script.working_title: Tirzepatide (Mounjaro) and Muscle: Where to Start Strength Training
script.hook_pattern: Counterintuitive claim + stakes and specificity ("about 5 of every 20 pounds lost weren't fat"), followed by an open loop (which type of exercise kept the least lean mass during dieting), paid off in "The exercise surprise"

scenes.narration: Lose twenty pounds on tirzepatide, and in the trial's body scans, about five of those pounds, on average, weren't fat.

visual.stat_label: of weight lost was lean mass (SURMOUNT-1 scan subgroup, adults without diabetes)

scenes.retention_device: Counterintuitive claim with a concrete number in the first 5 seconds

scenes.narration: That's not unique to this drug. It happens with almost any kind of weight loss. But it raises a question worth asking: how do you hold on to the muscle you have?

In the next few minutes, you'll see exactly what the big tirzepatide trial measured, what lean mass really is, and a guideline-based way to start strength training, even if you've never lifted anything heavier than a grocery bag.
And stay with me, because one trial tested three types of exercise in people who were dieting. The type that kept the least lean mass is one a lot of people start with.

visual.stock_query: three doors labelled with exercise icons

scenes.retention_device: Main open loop, paid off in The exercise surprise

scenes.narration: First, let's decode the jargon, because lean mass isn't what most people think it is.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card that promises a correction

scenes.narration: Researchers measure body composition with a DXA scan. You lie on a padded table while a scanner arm passes over you, using low-dose X-rays at two different energy levels.

visual.stock_query: relaxed patient on DXA scanner table

scenes.retention_device: Micro-scene that shows how the scan works

scenes.narration: Those beams split your body into three parts: fat mass, bone mineral, and lean mass.

visual.stock_query: body silhouette split into three colors

scenes.narration: Here's the catch. Lean mass isn't pure muscle. It also includes water, organs, skin and connective tissue.

visual.fact: Lean mass also includes water, organs, skin and connective tissue
visual.stock_query: jar filled with water drops organs muscle

scenes.narration: So when a scan says lean mass dropped, some of that is muscle, but not all of it. Headlines often treat the two as the same thing. They're not.
scenes.retention_device: Short punchy closing line before the section change

scenes.narration: Now, the trial. SURMOUNT-1 tested tirzepatide in 2,539 adults with obesity, or overweight with at least one weight-related condition, and without diabetes.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card that pays off the hook's source

scenes.narration: People were randomly assigned to weekly tirzepatide at 5, 10 or 15 milligrams, or to placebo, with roughly 630 to 640 people in each group. Everyone also got lifestyle counselling.

visual.stock_query: four groups of people at tables

scenes.narration: After 72 weeks, average weight loss was 15 percent of body weight on 5 milligrams, 19.5 percent on 10, and 20.9 percent on 15, versus 3.1 percent on placebo.

visual.stock_query: four bar chart columns with people

scenes.narration: Those figures count everyone assigned to each group, including people who stopped treatment early.
scenes.retention_device: Credibility beat: how the number was calculated

scenes.narration: But a scale can't tell you what was lost. So a subgroup of 160 people, 124 across the tirzepatide doses and 36 on placebo, also had DXA scans.

visual.stock_query: scale shrugging next to body scanner

scenes.retention_device: But/therefore turn that sets up the reveal

scenes.narration: Here's what the scans showed. With the three tirzepatide doses pooled, total fat mass fell by 33.9 percent, versus 8.2 percent on placebo.
Lean mass fell too: 10.9 percent on tirzepatide, versus 2.6 percent on placebo.
Put those together, and on tirzepatide the ratio of fat lost to lean mass lost was about three to one. Roughly three-quarters of the weight lost was fat.

visual.stat_label: fat lost to lean lost, tirzepatide

scenes.narration: So most of what people lost was fat. But about a quarter wasn't. And that's the part everyone's talking about.

visual.stock_query: spotlight on one quarter of pie

scenes.retention_device: Balanced framing that keeps the stakes

scenes.narration: But is that quarter caused by tirzepatide itself? This is where it gets interesting.
Losing some lean mass isn't new, and it isn't specific to GLP-1 medicines.

visual.stock_query: different diet plates side by side

scenes.retention_device: Chapter card that answers the cliffhanger

scenes.narration: For decades, obesity researchers have quoted a rule of thumb: when you lose weight, about one-quarter of it is fat-free mass.

visual.stat_label: widely cited share of weight loss: fat-free
visual.stock_query: old textbook with rule of thumb

scenes.narration: A 2014 critical review of that rule found it's a rough guide, not a law. It varies, for example with how much body fat someone starts with.
scenes.on_screen_text: A rough guide, not a law

visual.fact: A rough guide that varies between people

scenes.narration: Separate studies of calorie-restricted diets and bariatric surgery, not the tirzepatide trial, also report lean mass falling alongside fat.
Some researchers see part of this as an adaptation. A lighter body needs less muscle to carry it around.
In a 2024 JAMA viewpoint, three obesity researchers argued that for many people, weight-loss-related muscle loss may matter less clinically than headlines suggest.
But they also flagged groups where it may matter more, like older adults and people who already have low muscle mass.
So if some loss is normal, why bother protecting muscle at all? Because of what muscle does for you.
scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer before the section change

scenes.narration: Muscle isn't just for looks. It's one of your body's biggest players in handling blood sugar.
In lab studies where insulin is raised, skeletal muscle takes up roughly 80 percent of the glucose cleared from the blood.

visual.stat_label: insulin-stimulated glucose uptake by muscle (lab studies)

scenes.narration: Think of it as a big sponge for blood sugar. That matters a lot if you're living with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes.
Muscle also powers everyday life: climbing stairs, carrying groceries, getting up from a chair, and staying steady on your feet.
And strength is linked to survival. The PURE study followed nearly 140,000 adults across 17 countries, and lower grip strength was linked to a higher risk of death.
That's an observational link, not proof that a grip trainer adds years. But it fits a bigger picture: strength is a useful marker of health.

visual.fact: Grip strength is linked to survival, not proven to cause it

scenes.narration: The US guidelines link regular physical activity to lower risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes and several cancers, plus better sleep and mood.
So what kind of exercise protects lean mass best while you're losing weight? Time to pay off that promise from the start.
scenes.retention_device: Callback to the main open loop

scenes.narration: In 2017, a team published a clever trial in the New England Journal of Medicine.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card with a story opener

scenes.narration: They enrolled 160 adults aged 65 and older with obesity, split across four groups. Three groups got a weight-loss program plus a different exercise plan.
Aerobic exercise only. Resistance training only. Or both combined. The fourth group got no diet or exercise program, as a comparison.
After 26 weeks, all three exercise groups lost about 9 percent of their body weight. So far, a tie.

visual.stat_label: body weight lost, each exercise group, 26 weeks

scenes.narration: But lean mass told a different story. It fell about 5 percent with aerobic exercise alone, versus about 2 percent with resistance training and 3 percent with both.

visual.stock_query: three bar columns one taller drop

scenes.retention_device: Payoff of the main open loop

scenes.narration: So the plan that kept the least lean mass was cardio alone, the walking-and-treadmill approach a lot of people start with.
And on a test of everyday physical tasks, the combined group improved most: about 21 percent, versus about 14 percent in each single-exercise group.

visual.stock_query: older adult putting on jacket easily

scenes.retention_device: Second twist that opens the 'do both' idea

scenes.narration: One big caveat: these were older adults on a diet, not people taking tirzepatide. But it shows why guidelines recommend strength work alongside cardio, not instead of it.
So what does that look like for a real beginner? Let's build it.
scenes.retention_device: Forward hook into the practical section

scenes.narration: Here's what major guidelines recommend for adults in general. This isn't a plan proven on tirzepatide, but it's the best-supported place to start.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card with an honest hedge

scenes.narration: The World Health Organization and the US Physical Activity Guidelines agree: muscle-strengthening activities that work all the major muscle groups, on two or more days a week.

visual.quote: Adults should also do muscle-strengthening activities at moderate or greater intensity that involve all major muscle groups on 2 or more days a week, as these provide additional health benefits.
visual.attribution: WHO guidelines on physical activity and sedentary behaviour, 2020

scenes.narration: Alongside that, both recommend 150 to 300 minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity, like brisk walking.

visual.stat_label: minutes a week of moderate aerobic activity

scenes.narration: If that sounds like a lot, here's the good news. The US guidelines say some activity is better than none, and that inactive people should start small and build up gradually.
So start gently. Your first week might be two short sessions of a few simple moves.
Level one is your own bodyweight: sit-to-stands from a chair, wall push-ups, and glute bridges on the floor.
Level two adds resistance bands, which are cheap, light and easy to control. Level three, when you're ready, is weight machines or dumbbells.
The US guidelines name these as muscle-strengthening options: lifting weights, working with resistance bands, and bodyweight exercises like push-ups.
How many reps? The guidelines say one set of 8 to 12 repetitions per exercise is effective, and two or three sets may be more effective.

visual.stat_label: reps per set; 2–3 sets may help more

scenes.retention_device: Question to the viewer, answered with a number

scenes.narration: Choose a weight or band where the last couple of reps feel challenging but your form stays clean. Then, over the weeks, add a little: one more rep, one more set, or a slightly stronger band.
Machines are a handy middle step because they guide the movement. And if you're unsure about form, a physical therapist can show you.
If you have heart disease, joint problems or another health condition, check with your clinician before starting something new.
But training is only half the muscle equation. The other half is on your plate.
In 2025, four medical, nutrition and obesity organizations published a joint advisory on nutrition for people taking GLP-1 medicines for obesity.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card with an authority setup

scenes.narration: The American College of Lifestyle Medicine, the American Society for Nutrition, the Obesity Medicine Association, and The Obesity Society.
A central theme: get enough protein from a variety of foods, and pair it with physical activity that includes strength training, to help preserve muscle.
Because these medicines can shrink your appetite, protein can quietly drop off your plate. A simple habit is to include some protein at each meal.
Think eggs or Greek yogurt at breakfast, beans or lentils at lunch, and fish, chicken or tofu at dinner.
If you fill up fast, try eating the protein part of your plate first.
One important exception: if you have kidney disease, or your clinician has told you to limit protein, check with them before eating more.
A registered dietitian can turn this into a plan that fits your tastes, budget and health.
Now, what about the days you feel queasy and a workout is the last thing you want?
scenes.retention_device: Relatable question that opens the next section

scenes.narration: The most common side effects on the tirzepatide label are digestive, such as nausea, diarrhea, vomiting and constipation.
scenes.retention_device: Chapter card with a brief, honest side-effect line

scenes.narration: If they're bothering you, tell your prescriber. Adjusting your treatment is their call, not something to do on your own.
Clinical recommendations for GLP-1 side effects include eating smaller meals, eating slowly, stopping when you feel full, and going easy on high-fat foods.
For workouts, that might mean a light snack well before training instead of a big meal right before, and a gentler session on rough days.

visual.stock_query: banana snack and clock before gym

scenes.narration: Drink fluids through the day, especially after vomiting or diarrhea, unless you've been told to limit fluids. The label warns these side effects can cause dehydration, which can affect the kidneys.
If you have type 2 diabetes and also use insulin or a sulfonylurea, ask your care team about low blood sugar around exercise. The label notes a higher risk with those combinations.
And if you feel dizzy, faint or unwell during a session, stop, rest, and get medical advice if it doesn't settle.
You've got the science and the plan. One step left: the right questions for your team.
scenes.retention_device: Progress cue that opens the final section

scenes.narration: Bring these to your next appointment.
For your prescriber: Is strength training safe for me right now, and is there anything I should avoid?
For a dietitian: How much protein is right for me, given my kidneys, my appetite and my other conditions?
For a physical therapist: Where should I start, given my joints, balance and fitness level?
And don't stop or change your current medicines on your own. These medicines aren't right for everyone, and your care team can help you weigh it up.
Remember where we started? In the SURMOUNT-1 scans, about three-quarters of the weight lost on tirzepatide was fat. The other quarter is where recommended habits come in.
So here's your checklist. Strength training on two or more days a week, starting gently. Aerobic activity building toward 150 minutes a week.
Protein at each meal from a variety of foods, unless you've been told to limit it. Fluids through the day, unless you've been told to limit fluids.
Smaller, slower meals on queasy days. And your questions written down for your prescriber, dietitian or physical therapist.
These habits are recommended for adults in general. They haven't been proven to protect muscle on tirzepatide specifically, but they're a solid, evidence-based start.

visual.myth: Proven to protect muscle on tirzepatide
visual.fact: Guideline habits recommended for adults in general

scenes.narration: If you want the research decoded like this as new tirzepatide and muscle studies come out, subscribe to InforMed.
Tirzepatide is a prescription medicine. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
This script passes. I found nothing harmful or misleading, only 7 minor fixes.

The core numbers match their published sources:
- **SURMOUNT-1 (main trial):** 2,539 adults with obesity, or overweight with a weight-related condition, without diabetes. Groups of about 630–640 each. Weight change at 72 weeks: −15.0%, −19.5% and −20.9% on the three doses vs −3.1% on placebo, counting everyone assigned to each group.
- **SURMOUNT-1 body-scan (DXA) subgroup:** 160 people. Fat mass fell 33.9% vs 8.2% on placebo, and lean mass fell 10.9% vs 2.6%. About 3:1, or roughly a quarter of the weight lost as lean mass.
- **Villareal 2017 exercise trial (NEJM):** 160 adults aged 65+ with obesity. About 9% weight loss in every exercise group. Lean mass fell about 5% with aerobic only, 2% with resistance only and 3% with both. Physical performance improved 21% with both vs 14% with either alone.
- **Other studies:** PURE (nearly 140,000 adults in 17 countries), DeFronzo (muscle takes up about 80% of glucose when insulin is raised), Heymsfield 2014 (the "one-quarter" rule) and Conte/Hall/Klein in JAMA 2024.
- **Guidelines:** the WHO quote and the US activity guidelines (150–300 minutes a week, 2+ strength days, 1 set of 8–12 reps, some activity beats none).
- **Zepbound label:** digestive side effects, dehydration that can affect the kidneys, and low blood sugar when combined with insulin or a sulfonylurea.

The framing is careful. It keeps the trial population, explains that lean mass isn't only muscle, labels PURE as observational, says plainly that the Villareal trial was not a tirzepatide trial, and calls the habits "recommended, not proven on tirzepatide".

All the safety pieces are there: start gently, check with a clinician if you have heart disease or joint problems, a kidney caveat for protein, a fluid caveat, a low-blood-sugar note, don't change your medicines on your own, these medicines aren't right for everyone, and the prescriber line.

The minor fixes:
- The activity-guidelines link redirects; swap in the final address.
- Make the DXA scan description more precise.
- Show the scan-subgroup sizes for each group.
- Remove one unsupported "most people" line (s4, mirrored in s41).
- Describe the four organizations accurately.
- Remove two source tags I couldn't confirm.

I couldn't open the full text of the Neeland 2024 review (src2; behind a captcha and paywall) or confirm that the 2025 nutrition advisory says "protein at each meal". The fixes cover both by removing the source tags from those exact lines.

issues.problem: This link returns a 302 redirect to odphp.health.gov. Source lists should use the final, canonical address.

issues.claim: "using two low-dose X-ray beams" (source tag src2)
issues.problem: DXA measures X-rays at two energy levels, often from one source, so "two beams" is slightly off. I also couldn't confirm that src2 (a review of GLP-1 drugs and lean mass) describes how the scanner works.
issues.fix: Narration: "Researchers measure body composition with a DXA scan. You lie on a padded table while a scanner arm passes over you, using low-dose X-rays at two different energy levels." Set source_ids to [].

issues.claim: "160 participants in total, spread across the tirzepatide doses and placebo"
issues.problem: House rule: give group sizes per group, not as one combined number. The subgroup was 124 on tirzepatide (pooled) and 36 on placebo. This matters because the fat and lean figures in s15–s16 are pooled across the tirzepatide doses.
issues.fix: Narration: "But a scale can't tell you what was lost. So a subgroup of 160 people, 124 across the tirzepatide doses and 36 on placebo, also had DXA scans." On-screen: "DXA: 124 tirzepatide vs 36 placebo"

issues.claim: "The type that kept the least lean mass is the one most people reach for first." / "the walking-and-treadmill approach many of us default to"
issues.problem: No source supports "most people reach for cardio first". It is our own assumption stated as a fact.
issues.fix: s4: "The type that kept the least lean mass is one a lot of people start with." s41: "So the plan that kept the least lean mass was cardio alone, the walking-and-treadmill approach a lot of people start with."

issues.problem: The American College of Lifestyle Medicine is a lifestyle-medicine society, not a nutrition or obesity group, so the description is slightly inaccurate.
issues.fix: Narration: "In 2025, four medical, nutrition and obesity organizations published a joint advisory on nutrition for people taking GLP-1 medicines for obesity."

issues.claim: "A simple habit is to include some protein at each meal." (source tag src10)
issues.problem: I could confirm that the advisory stresses getting enough protein and doing strength training, but not that it says "at each meal". The per-meal tip should read as our own practical suggestion, without a source tag.
issues.fix: Keep the narration as written but set source_ids to []. Or split it: put "Because these medicines can shrink your appetite, protein can quietly drop off your plate" in a scene tagged src10, and put "One simple habit: include some protein at each meal" in its own scene with no tag.

issues.claim: "Lose twenty pounds on tirzepatide, and in the trial's body scans, about five of those pounds, on average, weren't fat."
issues.problem: The hook leaves out the population until s10. House rule: keep the trial population near the number. The on-screen "not fat" is acceptable because lean mass made up nearly all of the non-fat loss.
issues.fix: On-screen: "~1 in 4 lbs lost: lean mass". Stat label: "of weight lost was lean mass (SURMOUNT-1 scan subgroup, adults without diabetes)".
